https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/08/04/mes.text: Menü Kereső Mészárosék azt állítják, hogy órákkal azelőtt válaszoltak a Mavir levelére, mielőtt Magyar Péter beszólt nekik a Mavir központjából Gazdaság Csurgó Dénes Iván-Nagy Szilvia Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Magyar Péter hétfő este a Magyar Villamosenergia-ipari Átviteli Rendszerirányító Zrt. (Mavir) központjából jelentkezett be videón az energiahelyzetről, ezt az alkalmat pedig arra is felhasználta, hogy név szerint beszóljon Mészáros Lőrinc izocukorgyártó cégének , a Kall Ingredients Kft.-nek, amiért az még nem válaszolt arra, önként csökkenti-e az energiafelhasználását. Mészárosék azóta közölték, hogy ők már rég válaszoltak a megkeresésre , mire Magyar Péter beszólt nekik hétfőn este, a Telex kérdésére pedig a Mészáros-csoport azt is megírta egy válaszban, hogy pontosan mikor kapott levelet a Mavirtól a cég, és mikor küldték meg a választ. A cégcsoport korábbi sajtóközleménye szerint a válaszlevelükben azt vállalták, hogy a Kall Ingredients a kritikus időszakban az óránkénti lekötött kapacitáshoz képest legalább közel 10 százalékkal alacsonyabb energiafelhasználással fog működni. A Mészáros-csoport Telex kérdésére küldött válaszlevele szerint a Mavir augusztus 3-án hétfőn 12.20-kor kereste meg írásban a céget. A kommunikáció hivatalos elektronikus levélben történt. „Ezt követően a menedzsment haladéktalanul megkezdte a lehetséges megoldások számbavételét, majd a vállalat 15:28 órakor írásban elküldte válaszát” – írták Mészárosék. Magyar Péter videós bejelentkezése hétfő este 19:34-kor kezdődött. Megjegyezték, hogy a villamosáram visszavétele egy folyamatosan termelő üzem esetében sosem egyik pillanatról a másikra történik, „hanem előírásban megkövetelt eljárásrend szerint, amit az üzembiztonsági elvárásoknak és előírásoknak megfelelően be kell tartani”. A Mészáros-csoport a Telexnek azt írta, hogy vállalataik már a Mavir megkeresése előtt is tettek önkéntes fogyasztáscsökkentő lépéseket, a tevékenységi körükhöz, illetve működési sajátosságaikhoz igazodó intézkedéseket vezettek be. Az önkéntes vállalások elsősorban vízfelhasználás, hűtési, légkondicionálási, világítási és egyéb villamosenergia-felhasználó területeket érintettek, „továbbá több cégünknél az adminisztratív területen dolgozók home officeban történő munkavégzéssel járultak hozzá az energiatakarékossághoz.” Kerestük reakcióért a Miniszterelnökséget és a Mavirt is, érdemi válaszukról beszámolunk. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Several pro-Houthi men take part in a rally to recruit new fighters for the group in Sanaa on Wednesday. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Several pro-Houthi men take part in a rally to recruit new fighters for the group in Sanaa on Wednesday. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images Yemen Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.45 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen , approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government. The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador to Yemen , Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden. Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west. View image in fullscreen A Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter is seen purportedly firing at a Houthi position near Dhubab in Taiz. Photograph: Southern Giants Brigades/Reuters Houthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded. The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that the Houthis have stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”. Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved? Read more There has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims about Yemeni government advances issued at the beginning of the week. Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people. The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel. Southern Giants forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. The group is now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: BRUSSELS — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has expressed openness toward restarting free movement between the United Kingdom and the European Union as the two sides prepare for next month’s leaders’ summit. A return to free movement would not be a red line for talks, he suggested, as immigration trends had changed since the U.K. voted to leave the EU in 2016. However, Burnham said he would not “jump to a firm position” on the issue just yet. “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament,” he told the Sunday Times . Advertisement Advertisement “But at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now]. Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.” Burnham said at the Labour Party Conference in September that he is weighing different options for a reset of relations with the 27-country bloc. He did not elaborate in his conference speech on the options he would present — but different figures within Labour have argued for joining the EU single market, the customs union, or rejoining the bloc wholesale. Rejoining the single market would require the U.K. to sign up to the EU’s rules permitting free movement of people. His stance on freedom of movement marks a significant shift from the Labour Party’s 2024 manifesto , which ruled out a return to the single market, customs union or free movement, and comes one month ahead of a Nov. 20 summit where the EU and the U.K. hope to sign off on a set of agreements ranging from trade to climate regulations. In his interview with the Sunday Times, he set out his own red lines, adding that he “can’t see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen.”

https://praguemonitor.com/work-life/how-.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Applicants over 15 for a long-term visa or permit supply an extract from their country of citizenship and, on request, from countries where they spent over six months in the last three years. The extract should be no older than 180 days on the filing date, or less if it states a shorter validity (as of 2026; check MV), so timing is the main risk. The usual chain is: issue, apostille or legalisation, sworn translation into Czech, then file; EU documents may be exempt from the apostille. On this page 6 sections What the certificate is and what it is called From which countries The age limit is the trap The chain after issue Who orders it Practical problems Of all the papers in a residence application, the criminal-record extract is the one that most often expires while the rest of the file is still being assembled. It is cheap in most countries and slow in a few, it has a maximum age and it needs two further steps before a Czech clerk will look at it. Treat it as a project with a deadline, not as a form. What the Ministry of the Interior requires depends on your permit and nationality, and the list changes, so use the current document list for your application. What the certificate is and what it is called A criminal-record certificate is an official statement from a state authority about whether a person has criminal convictions recorded against them. The name differs: "police certificate", "certificate of good conduct", "criminal-record extract", "police clearance", "certificate of no criminal convictions". Some countries issue a short extract that says only that there are no entries; others issue a fuller summary. For Czech purposes, what matters is that the document is issued by the competent state authority, covers the right person and is accepted by the Ministry. Ask the Ministry or the embassy whether the version your country issues is acceptable. Some countries have more than one version. A police-held check can differ from a certificate from the central criminal register, and a certificate from a state or province can differ from a national one. Check which the Ministry wants. In the United Kingdom, for instance, a police certificate for overseas use is issued by a specific national office, and in the United States the FBI Identity History Summary is used, with an apostille from the US Department of State (our guide for Americans in Czechia covers it); verify both with the issuing office and the Czech embassy before ordering, because procedures change. From which countries The Foreigners Act asks applicants over 15 for long-term visas, long-term and permanent residence to document that they have no criminal record. The rule is an extract from the country of citizenship, and the Ministry or embassy may also ask for one from any country where the applicant spent more than six months in total during the last three years. If a country does not issue such a document, a sworn declaration ( čestné prohlášení ) can replace it (as of 2026; check MV and the embassy). If you have lived in several countries, make a list with dates early, because each extract has its own lead time and its own authentication. Czech authorities check their own record for applicants who have lived in Czechia. You do not usually need to bring a Czech extract for the Ministry; the Ministry obtains it. If you need a Czech criminal-record extract for use abroad, for example for a visa elsewhere, you can request one, and the Czech authority will issue it; the process and cost are on the Ministry of Justice's pages, and the extract can be apostilled for foreign use. Children under 15 are exempt. Spouses and adult family members have to supply their own. Our overview of family reunification and the guide to bringing a spouse show where it fits in a family application. The age limit is the trap Ministry and embassy instructions say supporting documents must be no older than 180 days on the day you file, with exceptions such as passports and civil-status certificates. Where the certificate itself states a shorter validity, often 90 days or three months in some countries, that shorter period applies (as of 2026; check MV and the embassy). A certificate that is too old on the day of filing will be rejected, regardless of how long the apostille took. Work backwards. Decide the filing date, which is the day of your embassy appointment, then subtract the time for translation, apostille and issue. Take a hypothetical case: you have an embassy appointment on 1 March. The sworn translation needs a week, the apostille two to three weeks, and the extract itself takes two weeks to arrive. Ordering on 1 January leaves a margin of about three weeks; ordering in early August risks an extract that has passed 180 days by the appointment, and a certificate with its own 90-day validity would already be out of date if ordered in early November. Timing the extract maximum age of an extract on the filing date, unless it states a shorter validity 180 days issue, apostille or legalisation, sworn translation 3 steps Source: Ministry of the Interior; Czech embassy instructions (as of 2026; check for your permit) Appointment slots can move, and a postponed appointment can push the filing date beyond the age limit. If you are close to the limit, ask the embassy whether a new extract is needed, and think twice before committing to non-refundable travel. The chain after issue The extract is a public document, and as such it usually needs authentication. If the issuing country belongs to the Hague Apostille Convention, you obtain an apostille from the competent authority. If not, the document goes through legalisation by the foreign ministry and the Czech embassy. Our guide to apostille and legalisation explains both and the EU exemption: Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 removes the formality for some EU documents, but ask whether the Ministry accepts the exemption for your file. After authentication, a court translator translates the extract into Czech. See sworn translations in Czechia for how to find one and what the finished bundle looks like. Documents in Slovak are treated more leniently in many Czech procedures; ask whether translation is needed. Ordering the extract List your countries and dates Country of citizenship, and any country where you spent more than six months in the last three years. Fix the filing date Use your embassy appointment as the deadline and count backwards. Request the right version Ask the issuing authority for the type accepted for use abroad, with fingerprints if required. Authenticate Apostille or legalisation, as the issuing country requires. Translate and file Sworn translation into Czech, bound to the authenticated extract, then submit within the age limit. Who orders it Usually you order it yourself, as the person named on it, because the issuing authority wants to confirm your identity. Some countries allow an authorised agent or a family member to apply for you with a power of attorney, which itself may need authentication. If you live in a different country from the one that issued your citizenship, check whether your own embassy can supply the extract. Do not pay a third party for a document that the authority issues for a small official fee unless you have a reason, such as a time pressure or a very slow system. Practical problems Fingerprints. Some countries require fingerprints taken by the police or at an accredited agency, and the process involves ink cards or digital scans. Residents abroad can have trouble finding an office; the issuing authority's website explains the alternatives. Identity details. The extract is issued for one name, date of birth and place of birth. If your passport shows a different spelling, a married name or a transliteration, bring evidence. Names must match across the file. Our checklist for your first month shows how often the same documents come back. Countries with slow systems. Some registries take weeks or months, or require an application by post or in person. Start there. Previous convictions. Some convictions can lead to a refusal, and the Foreigners Act and the Ministry's practice decide which, by type of offence, sentence and time elapsed. If you have a record, take legal advice before filing and do not leave it out; a concealed conviction that the Ministry finds is a worse problem than the conviction itself. Renewals and permanent residence. The extract may be required again at later stages; see how to renew a residence permit and permanent residence . Keep a record of what you submitted and when. Frequently asked questions Which countries' certificates do I need? Your country of citizenship and, if asked, countries where you spent more than six months in the last three years. Check MV and the embassy. How recent must the certificate be? No older than 180 days on the filing date, or less if the certificate states a shorter validity (as of 2026; check MV). Do I need to translate it? Yes, normally by a court translator into Czech, after the apostille or legalisation. Check whether a Slovak or EU document is exempt. Do children need one? Not under 15. Everyone older in the family needs their own. This is a general explainer, not legal or tax advice.
